title: Barger et al., Lancet Neurology 2014
citation: Barger, L. K., Flynn-Evans, E. E., Kubey, A., Walsh, L., Ronda, J. M., Wang, W., Wright, K. P., Jr., & Czeisler, C. A. (2014). Prevalence of sleep deficiency and use of hypnotic drugs in astronauts before, during, and after spaceflight: An observational study. *The Lancet Neurology, 13*(9), 904–912.
finding: Orders of magnitude for in-flight sleep; used to set the simulated mean of about 6.5 h.

title: Otsuka et al., Scientific Reports 2021
citation: Otsuka, K., Cornelissen, G., Furukawa, S., Kubo, Y., Shibata, K., Mizuno, K., Ohshima, H., & Mukai, C. (2021). Astronauts well-being and possibly anti-aging improved during long-duration spaceflight. *Scientific Reports, 11*(1), Article 14907.
finding: Sleep data in spaceflight; used with Barger 2014 to calibrate simulated sleep.

title: Norsk et al., Journal of Physiology 2015
citation: Norsk, P., Asmar, A., Damgaard, M., & Christensen, N. J. (2015). Fluid shifts, vasodilatation and ambulatory blood pressure reduction during long duration spaceflight. *The Journal of Physiology, 593*(3), 573–584.
finding: Reference for heart rate and blood pressure in flight: heart rate unchanged and blood pressure about 10 mmHg lower than on the ground. The simulated values are our own approximation.

title: NASA-STD-3001 Volume 1 (Rev C)
citation: National Aeronautics and Space Administration. (2023). *NASA spaceflight human-system standard: Volume 1—Crew health* (NASA-STD-3001, Vol. 1, Rev. C). Office of the Chief Health and Medical Officer.
finding: Requirement V1 4030 (section 4.8.2): a crewmember's total career effective dose from spaceflight radiation shall be less than 600 mSv, the same for all ages and sexes. Requirement V1 4031 (section 4.8.3): protect crewmembers from the design reference solar particle event (the October 1989 events combined) to less than 250 mSv effective dose. That 250 mSv is a design target, not a personal dose limit.

title: NASA OCHMO-TB-003 Habitable Atmosphere
citation: National Aeronautics and Space Administration. (2023). *Habitable atmosphere* (OCHMO-TB-003, Rev. A) [Technical brief]. Office of the Chief Health and Medical Officer.
finding: Technical brief derived from NASA-STD-3001 Volume 2 (Rev D), requirement V2 6003: defines the allowed oxygen range in the cabin air (inspired oxygen partial pressure). Our 92% SpO2 alert limit is our own design rule, not a NASA limit.

title: Zeitlin et al., Science 2013
citation: Zeitlin, C., Hassler, D. M., Cucinotta, F. A., Ehresmann, B., Wimmer-Schweingruber, R. F., Brinza, D. E., Kang, S., Weigle, G., Böttcher, S., Böhm, E., Burmeister, S., Guo, J., Köhler, J., Martin, C., Posner, A., Rafkin, S., & Reitz, G. (2013). Measurements of energetic particle radiation in transit to Mars on the Mars Science Laboratory. *Science, 340*(6136), 1080–1084.
finding: Dose-equivalent rate measured on the way to Mars (MSL RAD), about 1.8 mSv/day; used for the simulated transit rate.

title: Guo et al., Astronomy & Astrophysics 2015
citation: Guo, J., Zeitlin, C., Wimmer-Schweingruber, R. F., Hassler, D. M., Posner, A., Heber, B., Köhler, J., Rafkin, S., Ehresmann, B., Appel, J. K., Böhm, E., Böttcher, S., Burmeister, S., Brinza, D. E., Lohf, H., Martin, C., & Reitz, G. (2015). Variations of dose rate observed by MSL/RAD in transit to Mars. *Astronomy & Astrophysics, 577*, Article A58.
finding: Dose rate measured inside a spacecraft on the way to Mars, including short jumps during solar particle events; used as background for the simulated storm spikes. The size of the spikes is simulated.

title: Stahn et al., Scientific Reports 2017
citation: Stahn, A. C., Werner, A., Opatz, O., Maggioni, M. A., Steinach, M., Weller von Ahlefeld, V., Moore, A., Crucian, B. E., Smith, S. M., Zwart, S. R., Schlabs, T., Mendt, S., Trippel, T., Koralewski, E., Koch, J., Choukèr, A., Reitz, G., Shang, P., Röcker, L., . . . Gunga, H.-C. (2017). Increased core body temperature in astronauts during long-duration space missions. *Scientific Reports, 7*(1), Article 16180.
finding: Reference for body temperature in spaceflight. The 38.0 °C fever limit is our own design rule.

title: Lang et al., Journal of Bone and Mineral Research 2004
citation: Lang, T., LeBlanc, A., Evans, H., Lu, Y., Genant, H., & Yu, A. (2004). Cortical and trabecular bone mineral loss from the spine and hip in long-duration spaceflight. *Journal of Bone and Mineral Research, 19*(6), 1006–1012.
finding: Reference for bone loss in long-duration spaceflight (Bones and muscle zone).

citation: Battelino, T., Danne, T., Bergenstal, R. M., Amiel, S. A., Beck, R. W., Biester, T., Bosi, E., Buckingham, B. A., Cefalu, W. T., Close, K. L., Cobelli, C., Dassau, E., DeVries, J. H., Donaghue, K. C., Dovč, K., Doyle, F. J., Garg, S. K., Grunberger, G., Heller, S., . . . Phillip, M. (2019). finding: Earth consensus range for glucose targets (70 to 180 mg/dL). Not validated for spaceflight.

title: Gew et al., Eye 2026
citation: Gew, J., Hyder, Y. F., Grech, O., Brunstetter, T., Tarver, W., Mason, S. S., Gibson, C. R., Polk, J. D., Schneider, V. S., van Baalen, M., Mitchell, J. L., Yiangou, A., Mollan, S.
